speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, on Monday the Final Act of the international health conference and the constitution of the world health organization were signed at New York by fifty-one of the united nations and by nine other nations. The signature for Canada was made by the Minister of National Health, and Welfare and the Deputy Minister of Health, Doctor G. B. Chisholm. There were also signed an intergovernmental arrangement

establishing the interim commission of the world health organization and a protocol designed to transfer to the world health organization the functions and duties now performed by the office Internationale d'hygiene publique.
I now table copies of these documents, and so that hon. members may have before them the text of the constitution, I ask the consent of the house to have it printed as an appendix to Votes and Proceedings.
A resolution will be introduced at this session if time permits to provide for the approval of the constitution.
At this conference Canada had as advisers, in addition to officers of the government, Doctor T. C. Routley, C.B.E., General Secretary of the Canadian Medical Association, and two former presidents of the Canadian Public Health Association, Doctor C. W. MacMillan, Professor of Public Health at McGill University and Doctor A. Groulx, chief medical officer of the City of Montreal. These distinguished representatives of the medicaL profession were in constant attendance throughout the whole period of the conference, and the government wishes to express its warm appreciation and thanks for services rendered in this way to their country and indeed, to humanity.
Doctor G. B. Chisholm, Deputy Minister of Health, acted as rapporteur of the technical preparatory committee which prepared the draft of the constitution. He was also chairman of the important committee of the conference dealing with administration and finance. The great value of his services in connection with the conference has been recognized by his selection as executive secretary of the interim commission of the new organization which will be charged with the task of setting up the new organization. This has necessitated his resignation as deputy minister of health, which has been accepted, and Doctor G. D. W. Cameron has been appointed in his place. Doctor Cameron saw service in the last war, graduated in medicine from Queen's University, holds the diploma of Public Health and has been director of health services of the department.
Canada has been named as one of the eighteen nations to constitute the interim . commission, which will carry on the work of organization until the required twenty-six states have ratified the 'constitution.
By these instruments the foundation has been laid of a single wmrld health organization, whose object is "the attainment by all peoples of the highest possible level of health." By the preamble the parties to the constitution declared that "the following principles are
United Nations-World Health

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
basic to the happiness, harmonious relations and security of all peoples." The first principle was that "health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity."
The functions of the organization will be varied. There is a wide field where cooperative action between nations is necessary and where the organization itself through its executive board and general assembly can give leadership in the attainment "by all peoples of the highest possible level of health."
The conference was an outstanding success. It showed that in a matter of wide human interest like health, the nations could work together to establish a world organization on a sound foundation. The constitution of the world health organization, which has just been unanimously agreed to, is not a colourless compromise, but represents a constructive document of world-wide scope and immense human significance.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, I have looked into tibe question directed by the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Eraser) on Monday last to the Minister of Mines and Resources concerning a certificate required) to be signed by persons applying for passports to enable them to go to countries outside the western hemisphere. As the issuance of passports comes within the jurisdiction of the Department of External Affairs, possibly I can answer the hon. member's question. The answer may help the public to understand why the formality is being required.
As the hon. member knows, the transportation situation was particularly difficult immediately after the war and travel beyond the western hemisphere was restricted to certain categories of applicants. As conditions abroad improved, these categories were broadened from time to time, and in June of this year the screening of applications for travel to countries beyond the western hemisphere was dispensed with. While there is now no screening process, transportation facilities will nevertheless continue to be limited for some time, and the government feels that it is only fair to warn all persons proceeding overseas that this condition exists. The passport office has, therefore, been authorized to endorse passports for any country on demand provided that the applicant signs a statement that he realizes the difficulty of obtaining transportation. The statement also acknowledges that the applicant realizes that the issuance of a passport does noit obligate the government of Canada to undertake any responsibility with regard to his transportation. It is thus made perfectly clear to the applicant that he will﻿JULY 24, 1946
have difficult travel conditions to face in connection with which the government may not be able to help him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee rose last night it was considering resolution 2 of the Income War Tax Act. Before the committee begins its discussion may I remind hon. members that this is one of the committees of the whole, and paragraph 2 of standing order 58 reads as follows:
Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
It has been the custom in the past to allow general discussion on the first clause, but I would remind the committee that we are now on the second one, and all discussion should be relevant to that particular clause.

Paragraph (b) of resolution 2 has to do with the allowance for dependents. I should like to mention particularly the provision in regard to dependent children under sixteen years of age. In explaining the purpose of this resolution the Minister of Finance said on June 27, as reported at pages 2915 and 2916 of Hansard:
I should like to make it clear that this proposal assumes the universal payment of family allowances to all taxpayers with eligible children from January 1, 1947. A taxpayer with a child eligible for family allowances will be assumed for purposes of income tax to have received family allowances, and will be given the deduction from income of only $100 in respect of such child. Taxpayers who are not now claiming family allowances for children eligible for them should make application for them to commence in the new year when the proposed measure will take effect.
I should like to submit to the Acting Minister of Finance that this is a harsh proposal for a number of people who prefer not to take family allowances. Surely it is arbitrary on the part of the government to say to them, "you must take family allowances or forego both your right to family allowances and your right to the deduction." Why should it not be possible for the department to continue the present basis, under which the taxpayer who is eligible for family allowances will take his benefit either in the form of family allowances or in the form of the larger deduction in respect of the support of the dependent child? It may be that it is easier for the departments concerned, National Revenue, Finance and National Health and Welfare, to do it in the way that it is proposed in this resolution; but the government should look farther than that.
Income War Tax

In actual effect, what does it mean? It means that some wage earners and salary earners from whose earnings deductions have not been hitherto made at the source will now become subject to deduction of taxes at the source, and those who do not pay their income tax on that basis-for instance, the man who is working on a commission or any basis other than salary or wages-will lose deductions he has hitherto enjoyed, in that the government will insist, in effect, on paying him his family allowances, and will take from him a larger sum in quarterly instalments of income tax. That seems an involved way of carrying on government business. In fairness to the taxpayers I suggest that the government owes them the duty to permit them the choice they now have of taking either the family allowances or the larger deductions.

speakeroldname: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Acting Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Perhaps I had better say a word in answer to the comments which have been made by the hon. member for Eglinton. In the first place, of course, there is no compulsion on anyone to take family allowances. If the taxpayer is eligible to claim and receive family allowances, it is optional with him whether he does it or not; but under the system proposed 'by the resolution, if he fails to do it the exemption which he can olaim for his child will be only. $100. My hon. friend has pointed out-

That is in effect
compulsion.-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It is not compulsory. He forfeits a certain amount of money each year; the average is $72 per child-^that is perfectly true. There are serious administrative difficulties in adopting a system such as my hon. friend suggests-difficulties particularly for the employer, because he would have to have one deduction for those employees who receive family allowances, and another deduction for those who do not. There would be administrative difficulties for the tax department in ascertaining whether or not family allowances had been claimed. There would have to be a complicated exchange of information. In my view what is more serious is that it implies that there is something wrong in a taxpayer taking family allowances who is eligible to receive them. It is true that on balance in the higher income bracket the taxpayer derives no net advantage from claiming family allowances under the system as it stands to-day. Under our proposed system, of course, he does, and' taking into account all the factors, the greater ease of administration so far as the employer and the tax department is concerned, and the fact

that parliament 'has approved the principle of family allowances, has declared that it is a desirable principle, I suggest it is not imposing any heavy burden on a man who is receiving five or six or seven thousand dollars a year to make a claim and1 receive the cheque once a month. There may be some practical disadvantage in the fact ttha/t his wife receives it instead of himself, but that is beside the point.

I take it that the government has made up its mind on this matter.
' The minister says that there is no compulsion. I say there is, in effect and in practice, compulsion. The government is saying to any individual who has Children eligible for family allowances: Apply for and take your family allowances, or you forfeit both your right to family allowances and your right to $200 of deduction in respect to the maintenance of that child. That is in effect compulsion.
The minister also says parliament has approved the principle of family allowances, and he goes on to conclude that therefore everybody ought to take them. I say, Mr. Chairman, there ought to be a measure of freedom allowed in a case of that kind; but that measure of freedom is to be taken away from those who do not choose to accept the family allowances by the proposal now before us, and I submit that is a definite interference with reasonable liberty on the part of these taxpayers involved. The fact that parliament has approved the principle of paying family allowances to those entitled is no reason why parliament should say to every taxpayer in this country, "You must take the family allowances or you lose the benefit of a deduction of $200 in respect of each child of yours under sixteen years of age."
I make this observation on the administrative problem involved. In his remarks I think the minister has placed a high premium on the ease of administration.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Ease for the employer, too.
I emphasized that, as well as ease for the taxpayer.

All right. I am speaking now of the minister's remarks in reference to ease of administration in the department, and I may refer to the employer in a moment. The minister has placed a high premium on ease of administration in the department, when that ease is to be carried to the lengths proposed in this resolution. What does it mean in effect? It means the government is making people take a larger income by accepting benefits from the government, and making them pay higher taxes.	,

speechtext: No.

Certainly that is what it amounts to. It means the taxpayer is being called upon to accept from the government on the one hand, and to give back to the government on the other, because his tax is going to be higher.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, or should know, the family allowances are not included in the taxable income.

It comes down to this, that the taxpayer will be paying higher taxes because he will get a lower deduction in respect of his children. Surely the sensible thing to do is to allow the taxpayer the choice. Let him have the right to take the family allowance or the right to take the higher deduction in respect to the maintenance of the children. Surely if the government is going to say to the individual, "Take the family allowance and pay a higher tax, because your deduction in respect to your children is being lowered by $260," it is simply creating two transactions which I submit are unnecessary. It is carrying the ease of the department in simplified administration to the point where I think it is done with less than adequate consideration for common sense and for the rights of the taxpayers. I sometimes think, Mr. Chairman, if that proverbial man from Mars dropped down on this earth and heard the Canadian government saying to a taxpayer, "You accept this cheque we are handing you and then turn around and pay us higher amounts in quarterly instalments or by way of deduction from your salary or wage, and keep that circle going " he would prefer to return to Mars, thinking we were a pretty crazy people.
I have one final observation about the other point made by the minister. He touched on the simplification of the task of the employer in respect to making deductions. Well, Mr. Chairman, the government gets out forms; there seems to be no lack of them. Why should it be an insuperable obstacle in this instance? Why not say to the employer: If the employee chooses to accept the family allowance, this is the form to use. On the other hand if the employee choses not to take the family allowance but to take the deduction of $300 in respect of each child under sixteen years of age, form No. 2 should
be used. Surely there is no great load cast on the employer in that respect. I can only conclude that the ease of the department in respect to family allowances in administering the Income War Tax Act is being exalted above the fair rights of the individual taxpayer.

My objection to the provision is not one of convenience but one of principle. I object to being put into a class of government annuitants whether I wish to be or not. I object to a government making me a beneficiary of the state whether I wish to be or not. It is the violation of that elementary principle of liberty that I object to here. If I am not content to become an annuitant of the state the penalty is that I lose a direct benefit to which I am entitled as the father of a family. That is significant of an era which unfortunately is not new to hon. gentlemen opposite. There was a time when we looked upon the Liberal party as a Liberal party, a party which adhered to the doctrine of Liberalism, freedom, and respect for individual liberty. To-day we find that doctrine violated in almost every measure coming before this house. When we are told that, whether we will it or not, whether we need it or not, we must accept money which the government offers us or be fined, I say that is a denial of the elementary principles of which we as Canadians have been proud and of which hon. gentlemen opposite have held themselves out as the great protectors and advocates. This instance in itself is not of grave importance, but it is indicative to me of an attitude which is contemptuous of individual freedom. I resent it and I object to it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Perhaps I might deal with one subject at a time. I have no desire to comment on my hon. friend's exposition of the principles of Liberalism, because I have never looked upon him as an outstanding expert in that field. On the question raised by the hon. member for Eglinton, there is one fact that perhaps he has overlooked: that is, that it may well be in the interests of the taxpayer to receive the family allowance rather than rely on the exemption. There are bound to be a good many marginal cases where it is impossible for a man to know in advance what his income is going to be for a particular year. If he were to follow the system we
Income War Tax

followed last year and exercise an option as to whether or not he receives the family allowance relying on his being in an income bracket which would mean that it would be of no benefit to him, in the result during the year it might well prove that his income would fall below that figure and it would turn out that he had made a choice that was to his disadvantage.
There is no greater compulsion exercised here than in asking a man to declare in his income tax return whether he has children of an age which entitles him to the exemption. In other countries in which family allowances are in force there is no option; family allowances are paid on a universal basis to taxpayers who are eligible to receive them. Taking all the factors into account the government has come to the conclusion that the system which is proposed under the terms of this resolution is one which is in the interest of the taxpayers and of the government, which after all is the government of the people.
Would the minister be good enough to mention the countries in which these allocations are forced upon people whether they wish them or not?

The United Kingdom,
Australia and New Zealand.
They all have socialistic governments.

Far be it from me to come to the defence of the present government, but I listened with some amazement and amusement to the professions of principle propounded by my eloquent friends to the right, when they said they were forced into the position of becoming annuitants of the state whether they wished to be or not. I should like to remind 'the house of what took place quite commonly throughout parts of this country in the early years of the war when the government was pressed for funds to prosecute the war. Many citizens in this and in other countries objected to taking interest on moneys lent for the prosecution of the war. I have many friends in that category. They lent their money to the government without any return of interest, because their principles were such that they would not permit themselves to receive profit from the war. My good friends to the right are not prepared to stand by their professed principles, when to do so would cost them a few dirty pennies. It seems to me that they are off on the wrong foot this morning.
However, I did not rise particularly to take issue with them on this matter, although I feel it keenly. I rose ito ask the minister what

constitutes married status. I receive letters from time to time from married men who are earning their incomes in this country, but whose dependents are abroad. Owing to circumstances beyond their control, during the war years they were unable to remit moneys to their families. I believe that under income tax regulations this prevented their considering themselves as married persons for income tax purposes. Would the minister explain what relief a married taxpayer might have in the event of his permitting someone else to assume temporarily the obligations for the support of his family abroad?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The regulations with respect to dependents of a class to which the. hon. member refers are found in rule 3 of section 2 of the first schedule to the Income War Tax Act. The section reads as follows:
A taxpayer may deduct $150 from the graduated tax otherwise payable by him in any year under this section if, during the taxation year, such taxpayer was-
(a)	a married person who supported his spouse and whose spouse was resident in any part of His Majesty's dominions or in a country contiguous to Canada, or, residing elsewhere, was a subject or citizen of a country associated or allied with Canada in the conduct of the war which commenced in September, nineteen hundred and thirty-nine, and was prevented by reason of such war, or prohibited by law, from entering or landing in Canada.
That covers the wife or husband who is in another country, the taxpayer residing here. Then, under the heading of "children," paragraph (b) refers to-
(b)	a person with a son or daughter wholly dependent upon him for support, if the son or daughter was, during the taxation year,
(i)	under eighteen years of age;
(ii)	eighteen years of age or over and dependent by reason of mental or physical infirmity; or
(iii)	under twenty-one years of age and a student at a secondary school, university or other educational institution.
This paragraph gives the same residence qualifications as apply to the wife or husband. I do not know whether that answers my hon. friend's question. If it does not, perhaps I might add that it would be a bit easier to discuss this question when the bill is before us. On the other hand, if he cares to pursue it further at this time, I shall be glad to try to clear the matter up.
I should like to know whether the fact that it was impossible, because of exchange regulations, to send the money abroad, prevented such a married person from being classified as such.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am advised that in cases where it was impossible to remit moneys to foreign countries-as, for example, in the case

Income War Tax
of China-the departmental practice 'has permitted a trust fund being set up here into which moneys can be paid, irrevocably. That would avail as justifying a claim for dependency, which of course would mean that some other arrangements would have to be made in the meantime for the support of the person abroad. I am informed that that is permitted under departmental practice.
That regulation is in effect?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion which has taken place respecting the effect of family allowances in our income tax schedule. I am hoping that some hon. members are not taking this too lightly.
I have had experience in the administration of income tax regulations, and I believe I know something of what the minister and his staff would be facing. I do not blame the officials of the income tax branch for seeking some relief for themselves, as well as for the taxpayers. I know what the job is. But I know, too, that there are fairly large groups of people who, because of deep convictions, are not accepting family allowances. Their convictions will not allow them to do so, because they have always had a spirit of independence. Those same substantial groups of people have taken the same view with respect to relief. Over the years they have cooperated among themselves to remove their numbers from the relief rolls of the countries in which they live. As I have said, that was done to maintain so far as possible under existing circumstances that spirit of independence which, it seems to me, is of great importance in any people. Under the new income tax proposals we are going to kill that spirit, because we are going to force those who by conviction have refused to become wards of the government in any respect, to accept family allowances, or in the alternative to be penalized to the extent of $72 per child by way of extra taxation.
I point that out because to my mind it is important. I should not like to see anything done which would destroy the independent spirit of any group of people, I do not care who they are. I would rather by all means do everything in my power to assist the government or the administrators of the Income War Tax Act to find a way by which they could give those people a choice in the matter. If this is humanly possible, let us find that way.
I am not now speaking against family allowances, because I have always felt that they were a good thing. But I certainly do
not like to see anything done that would destroy such a splendid spirit as we find among several groups of people, with one substantial group of which in Canada I am familiar.

I find it difficult to
understand that argument, coming from my hon. friend, because, as I understand it, the theory of my hon. friend is that everyone in the country should receive a dividend from the state.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Of $25 a month.
Both millionaire and pauper. I must confess I find it very difficult to follow his argument.
You would, because you believe in compulsion.

I do not believe in compulsion. I say to the hon. member that his former leader stated categorically that dividends would be paid to millionaire and pauper; I remember the phraseology very well. Apparently the intention was that every millionaire would receive it as well as every pauper. However, I am not dealing with that at the moment.
It seems to me that the net result of this provision is that it does not make any difference whatsoever to the individual whether he accepts the family allowance or not. The point is that it places everyone in the country on a basis of equality, and on the basis of equality, not on the basis of compulsion, I believe it should be supported by hon. members
It is all very well to talk about interference with the liberty of the subject, but I get a little nettled when I hear people talk about the liberty of the subject who when they were in power compelled hundreds of thousands of people to stand in line and ask for pittances. There never was a time in the history of this country when people were so regimented and compelled to accept poverty as when my hon. friends were in power from 1930 to 1935. To hear this kind of thing about this budget seems to me to be fantastic.
There are two things I think I must answer to-day. I can quite understand what the leader of the C.C.F. has said, because his whole programme is based on compulsion.
It is based on the liberty of the individual. These are the compulsory people on my right.

In the first place, the Social Credit group has never offered a programme based upon compelling anyone to accept any-
Income War Tax

thing. Whether or not a person accepts the dividend is his own business. He must register for it, and he has to make known his readiness to accept it. If he does not want to accept and if he does not want to register, he will not have to take it

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The same applies to family allowances.

The second point is this. As to compelling people to accept poverty, that is quite a different matter from compelling them to accept any person's or party's formula for getting out of poverty. Our whole programme is based upon choice. The individual has complete freedom to choose whether or not he will take a certain action. We have always supported the principle of family allowances, but we certainly do not want to lend our hand to making them compulsory. I am not saying that that principle is exactly the principle the minister has in mind, but I do say that the arrangement now being worked out does not give the people any choice except on a penalty. That is the thing that counts.
We believe in the distribution of the tax load according to ability to pay-I think we can all accept that principle. But you are not arranging the tax load according to ability to pay if you force people to accept family allowances as a condition of receiving a tax reduction. That is the principle I take exception to. Does the minister not think it is a serious matter to force an apparently substantial group of citizens who have deep convictions against the acceptance of family allowances into the position either of registering for them against their convictions or, in the alternative, of losing $72 per child?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Perhaps I might just say a word on this question of compulsion. In the first place, under our income tax law as it now stands and as it has stood for some years, those of us with incomes above a certain level have in fact been receiving family allowances. I have received a tax credit each year on my income tax of $108 for each of my three children. That was a form of family allowance to me as a taxpayer of $9 per month. It was not called a family allowance, but I was given a tax credit which meant that I paid $108 less tax every year for each one of my three children because they were under a certain age.
In reply to the impassioned plea of the hon. member for Stanstead that he did not want to be forced to accept anything he did not want to accept, let me point out that hon. gentlemen opposite have advocated old age pensions at sixty-five years of age without 
a means test. The other day I read through the statement made by the leader of the opposition on May 15 of last year when he advocated just such a policy. I cannot see any difference between an old age pension at sixty-five without a means test, payable to millionaire and pauper alike, and the payment of family allowances for all Canadian children under sixteen years of age.
I am advised that at the present time there are approximately 3,350,000 children for which family allowances are being paid, and that the change will add only about 150,000 to 175,000 children to the rolls. I cannot agree with the hon. member for Peace River that this is an objectionable form of compulsion. I do not think there is any more compulsion in it than to ask a man to declare in his income tax return whether he has children under sixteen years of age in order to get a S10S tax credit for each child. I understand that my hon. friend's group have advocated that we should pay old age pensions to all people over sixty-five years of age without a means test. If one is in favour of the principle of family allowances, and it has been endorsed by the house-I have yet to see a single hon. member stand up in his place and oppose it-[DOT] then I say that no one should have any objection to filing a formal claim.

May I have an answer to my question? I did not attack the principle at all, but I ask the minister, does he not think it a serious matter to force family allowances upon a substantial group of people who by conviction are against them, or put them in the position of being penalized to the extent of $72 per child?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I can answer that quite easily. Family allowances are part of the law of the land. If any citizen, by conviction or otherwise, feels that he does not want to accept this payment of $72 per year, that is his inalienable privilege as a British subject. However, he must be prepared to forfeit some monetary advantage because of his conviction. I do not think it is an improper use of government power to say that in common with millions of other citizens 'he should accept it, or if he does not, because of one reason or another, see fit to do it, that he should.

Some things have become clearer in the course of this discussion. Let us examine some of them for a moment. In the first place, the Acting Minister of Finance has said that family allowances are part of the law of the land, but I do not think it is the Jaw of the land that those who are eligible for family allowances must accept them or

Income War Tax
lose. Surely the basis of our present family allowances is that people with children under sixteen years of age are entitled to a monthly payment in respect'of each child if they choose to receive it. But now the government has tacked something on to that, and it says: Whether you like it or not, you must take that Benefit, you must apply for it and accept it from the government each month or you are going to lose certain benefits. The minister has said that after all there is no difference. He says, speaking for himself, "I in effect was receiving the family allowance". I controvert that principle entirely. The minister was not receiving a family allowance; the minister was enjoying a right given to him by the law of this land, either to accept the family allowance, and forgo certain deductions, or to take those deductions.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I had that right before there was any family allowance.

That right should be enjoyed by anyone. The minister is asking that parliament give to his personal judgment -his own preference, apparently, as it is now -the force of law for all citizens. He says: I think it is better that everyone should take the family allowance; therefore we are going to make everyone take the family allowance, and we are going to make everybody pay more income tax because we are going to reduce his deduction accordingly. I say that that is an evasion of the rights of the individual. It means that the government has made up its mind that everybody is to become the ward of the state-an annuitant, to use his own expression, whether he wishes it or not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I did not use the word "annuitant"; that was your friend from Stan-stead.

And it does not influence me in the least to take a view in favour of a resolution of this kind to see the leader of the C.C.F. rise and give it such vociferous support. If we want any better proof of the fact that inherent in this resolution is compulsion, you need no better evidence of it than the support given it to-day by the leader of the C.C.F.
Oh, how ridiculous!

I do not know when gentlemen sitting to your right, Mr. Chairman, are going to wake up to the fact that they are being led down the path by the C.C.F., when they go on welcoming so enthusiastically, as they always do, the way in which the leader of the C.C.F. comes to the government's rescue, as he so often does.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The Tories favour
reaction; that is the whole story.

If the Minister of Veterans Affairs has now decided that he is going to talk in the same tone as his colleagues, and not talk in different tones as he was doing on housing not so long ago, perhaps we can pay some attention to what he is saying.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I was here long before you were heard of.
If the Minister of Veterans Affairs goes on speaking as he is doing on the subject of the "aftermath", somebody one of these days is going to write finis to his career.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Are you against family allowances?
I am in favour of a system under which people will be allowed to accept family allowances, or not to take them without having a club held over their heads.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Tory reaction.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Go back to the eighteenth century where you belong.

It is too much to expect consistency from the Liberal party; and as for the leader of the C.C.F., he is living in the events of fifteen years ago. The Progressive Conservative party is living in modern times; it does not continue to live in the dark days of the ninteen-thirties.

When your party
was in power.

The Liberal party was
also in office in those days, and hon. members opposite can take what happiness they can get out of raking up the misfortunes of the people who suffered in this country then, as they suffered in every country in the world during the depression. So far as we are concerned we have learned some lessons from the experience of this country along with other countries in those days. I wish my hon. friend the leader of the C.C.F. would learn some lessons too.

Get a new record.

I should be glad to give the answer. I have repeatedly said that I am in favour of a system of family allowances; I always have been, but not on the basis of holding a gun to people's heads and saying to everybody: "You have got to take it-or else." For the benefit of the leader of the C.C.F., who is still living back in the early thirties, I should like to give him a quotation from a speech delivered by a man whom, perhaps, my hon. friend the leader of the C.C.F. may yet succeed as leader of the Liberal party.
Hear, hear.

over there.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Which resolution are we
on?

The speech to which I
am referring was made by the present Prime Minister of Canada when he was still leader of the opposition, in a hectic election campaign, on October 1, 1935.
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH:	Away back
there in the thirties!

I am giving this for the
benefit of the C.C.F., who have thrown up references to that period. This speech was made in Winnipeg. Making all due allowances for the fact that the Prime Minister delivered this speech in the heat of an election campaign-and we know that his speeches in the heat of election campaigns do not always jibe with the things he has said in this house, or with some of the things his cabinet ministers have been saying and parrotting since-this is what the Prime Minister said, as reported by the Canadian Press:
"I say that in making these promises Mr. Bennett set an example-"
He was speaking of Mr. Bennett's reform legislation in 1935; and if any members of the C.C.F want to say that they are opposed to that legislation I shall be glad to give them the opportunity.
". . . in making these promises Mr. Bennett set an example that is thoroughly immoral and

thoroughly wrong and which, if it is followed in the future, will lead to the ruination of this country."
"Where is the difference," asked Mr. King, "between offering a great body of people $25 a month and going into a man's home and putting $25 into his hand in exchange for his vote?"
And then there was an interjection:
"Bribery," came a voice from the gallery.
"Someone said bribery," said Mr. King. "I say any party which seeks to obtain office by offering money out of the public treasury, whether in the form of cash or in the form of projects to benefit certain persons, is departing from the only basis on which you can keep a nation straight in regard to the administration of public affairs."
When you add to that, Mr. Chairman, the element of compulsion, I say that this government is trying to thrust down the throats of the people benefits which ought to be available to them if they want to take them, but as to Which they should have an opportunity of making a choice, as they have to-day, instead1 of being compelled to take these family allowances. It does not seem to matter one iota to hon. gentlemen opposite that they are going to continue with this apparently endless process of building up a bureaucracy, creating more transactions for the government, making people more dependent on the government. Here is what it comes down to. The Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar have made up their minds that they prefer to see people compelled to take the family allowance-not given a choice. So far as I am concerned I insist that the principle is sound, and should be observed, that people shall still have the opportunity of saying whether they choose to take the deduction or whether they choose to take the family allowance.

May I just say one word? The hon. gentleman who has just spoken threw in an innuendo when he quoted from a former speech of the Prime Minister. Whatever I may think of the Liberal party,
I hope that among its own membership it could- find a successor to the Prime Minister and not have to follow the example of the Tory -party, who hunted from one end of this dominion to the other and then had to accept a gentleman who had always been opposed to them.
A pretty successful hunt.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: "Strike one!"
The marriage is complete.

I appreciate what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has said about Tory leadership, [DOT]which must have reached rock bottom, because for the second time

Income War Tax
they have looked to the Liberal party to lead them. The two last leaders of the Tory party were former Liberals. However, that having been said, I rise as a peace maker for the second time in my parliamentary career, and I wish to absolve all my colleagues in the house, those belonging to all parties and groups. I will say that if they were not so careless at times we would not be in such a jam.
I have here a paper which was widely distributed during the election of 1935. It is entitled "Taxes." It was distributed by the Liberal party, and the one who was responsible for it was the member for Temiscouata, because he was asked by the member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) to prepare a list of taxes imposed by R. B. Bennett and his government, to serve as political propaganda during the election. It was my deep conviction that the Liberal party would come back to the taxation that existed before 1930 that caused me to prepare that list. The list gave all the taxes imposed by Bennett during the five years of his regime, and I expected them all to be erased, to be struck out by the Liberals, so that we would return to the happy days prior to 1930. That was my purpose, and the paper was widely distributed throughout the country. Those figures can be found in Hansard. If hon. members are doubtful about it they may go to Hansard of 1935, where they will find a list of the taxes imposed by the Bennett government from year to year, from 1930 to 1935 inclusive.
There was the sugar tax, and there were many other taxes. They were all to go, but none of them has gone. I will show what comes under this heading of taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Why don't you read it?

I have a French copy, but it was published in English as well. I will read part of it to show that before 1930 the government thought more of man-power, especially young man-power, than it did afterwards. I remember a speech which the hon. member for Peel delivered on March 3, 1943, when the social legislation was brought down. He spoke after the Prime Minister and said that when the war was over we would have to pay more attention to man-power. More attention should have been paid to manpower at that time, and always, because manpower is the greatest wealth of the country- not only gun flesh, bodies to be slaughtered, but brains with which to think, brains to help to get the country out of the hole in which it is. I have the greatest respect for my fellow citizens and I believe that all the gold mines in the country, all the inanimate wealth, all
the deposits in the banks, are as nothing compared to a brain that is working normally, the brain of a child or the brain of a grownup. Therefore I appeal to the brains and the intelligence of my colleagues when I speak to them now, and I hope that they will be conscious of their responsibility.
Let us see what happened. The exemption from income tax for married couples in 1930 was $3,000 and for single persons it was $1,500. In 1932 Bennett reduced the exemption for married persons from $3,000 to $2,400 and for single persons from $1,500 to $1,200. Then it became much worse from 1933 to 1935. The exemption was reduced for married persons from $2,400 to $2,000 and for single persons from $1,200 to $1,000, while for children it was reduced from $500 to $400. Hon. members must remember that until then the exemption for young children who were dependents was $500. To-day it is a miserable pittance compared to what it was then, because at that time man-power was better regarded than it is to-day.
Think of it-a reduction from $500 to $400. Everyone complained at the time. I said it was wrong, and I said so with sincerity because I hoped that my party, the Liberal party, would return to the old traditions which I knew before Bennett came to power. And now we have the same rule as when Bennett was in power-and I do not apply that reproach to Mr. Elliott, the deputy minister of taxation, or to the taxation branch of the government, but to the crazy fools who made the financial policies of this country, and who think only of destroying the purchasing power of individuals. I do not understand why the leader of the C.C.F. and the member for Eglinton, both well gifted colleagues, talk about compulsion. Each tax is a compulsion. Each tax destroys the purchasing power and destroys the personality of one man. Everyone will agree with that. Why single out any tax when all taxes are alike?
We must consider the cause of taxation, the foolish expenditures that are made. But we heard of extravagance in the amendment that was defeated yesterday, the amendment, proposed by the Progressive Conservative party. They are thrifty of cents but they are ready to waste billions by enriching other countries at the expense of their own. They do not see that. They do not see the foolish extravagance of giving away billions of dollars at the expense of our own people, but when it comes to cents and a few small dollars, they are economical, and they complain about extravagance.
Income War Tax

What hypocrisy! Why are we here month after month? It is more than two months since I decided not to speak, but I came here just to say a few words about the seven and a half billions that have not been accounted for. They may have been lost at Bikini and perhaps we shall hear about them to-day when the submarine bomb explodes. Perhaps it will come up to the surface. We hear much about active assets, and I was told that the $450 million that was given for the air force of Great Britain was an active asset. What is more foolish than that? And yet we hear intelligent people indulging in that idle talk day after day, discussing the effect without ever trying to remove the cause. The only way to remove the cause is for the members of the House of Commons to come to their senses and to see through the thick fog of prejudice and propaganda, to see clearly what is the interest of this country, and to make up their minds about it and decide to do something at last for the Canadian people.
The officials of the income tax branch are not responsible for these foolish expenditures; those who are responsible are the ones who have made the policies of the government, those silly policies which I condemn with all the power of my voice and the sincerity of my heart. Those who are responsible are those who have given us bureaucracy. Why should the members of any party complain about bureaucracy when we have so many Charlie McCarthy to the Bergens of the west block? There they are; they are marvellous people. We must listen to them. They are doctors honoris causa; they com? from Queen's; they come from Toronto. They have been to Oxford, they have been to Cambridge, and it gives them a lustre, a kind of satin finish which makes them acceptable to all. And any one of those fools has more influence on the Minister of Finance than any member of parliament. Their word is the word of the gospel. They have landed here; they were landed in Ottawa by Bennett, by flattering his vanity, his immense vanity, by telling him that the North American continent was not fair to him, that he should be doctor of laws honoris causa of all universities on this continent; that he should swell up, that he should be just as big as the greatest giant who ever lived, a giant physically, mentally, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera.
What has been done for the farmer? I am sick of hearing my colleagues complaining of bureaucracy and doing nothing to curb it. The way to curb it is not to take away young people or young girls or boys who are stenographers 
or minor clerks. The thing to do is to cut the head off the snake. I am like St. Patrick; I follow his example. The first thing he did in evangelizing Ireland was to expel the snakes. I want the snakes to be expelled from office in Ottawa, the dangerous ones, those who are responsible for bringing this country to the position in which it is, of destroying economy, of destroying private initiative. They shall go. It is because of social parties that they do not go. Mrs. So-and-So meets Mrs. So-and-So, the wife of this eminent cabinet minister, and Mrs. So-and-So, the wife of this indispensable deputy, is very friendly with Mrs. So-and-So, who is in the social and personal column every day of the year. That is that. And who has to pay for it? The farmer has to pay for it; the man in overalls has to pay for it. Everyone has to pay for it. Here we are listening to it and indulging in shadowboxing. Is it the C.C.F. who are responsible for compulsion? Yes, they are responsible for compulsion. Is it the Tory party? Yes, it is the Tory party. Is it the Liberal, party? It is the Liberal party, and it is the Social Cred-iters. They are responsible-
No.

No, it is not? I do not think anyone is responsible for compulsion, because I have absolved all my colleagues. I referred to the discussion which took place in the house. It is the constant drawing of the red herring across the trail. The red herring becomes the political football; so it goes; time marches on; hon. members are satisfied when they say something cruel to the other party, and it usually comes back like a boomerang. Time passes. There are no reductions in taxes because the expenditure remains the same. How long have I to repeat the same thing to my colleagues?-because I do not consider that they are bereft of intelligence. I boost them every time I have the opportunity to do so; I want to wake them up. How is it that the English speaking audiences whom I have the honour to address all over the country are ready to think their own thoughts? I do not want to convey any of my thoughts to my colleagues; what I want them to do is to stop and think of the tremendous responsibilities of R. B. Bennett when he installed in the Bank of Canada and in the west block these men who have the power of life and death over all Canadian citizens.
I am not bigoted; I am not against the Jews. I believe that the Jews who are Canadians should have the same rights as all others, but on the other hand I do not see why the Jew should have more rights than the Canadian. I cannot understand how it is that one

Rasminsky, one of those who built up the bureaucratic structure, not long ago in a committee of the house refused to give information to members of parliament. He knew something that no one else knew with the exception of the Minister of Finance. Is it fair? I am not bigoted because I speak in this way; I am not to minimize -the rights of any Canadian citizen. I want them to be free and happy in this great country. But I do not see how it is that one man, whether he belongs to one race or another-if he were French Canadian I would denounce him just as bitterly as I denounce Rasminsky-how is it that one man is so secret, has a mystery which he will not give to others? These are the people who built up this chain of mountains of taxation, and we go on like that. What will be the way out? Did hon. members ever think of it? I believe in private initiative; I believe in the savings of the people. Everyone remembers -the progress that communism made in France because of the devaluation of the franc. be a heavy burden on him at that time. I have no doubt the
minister realizes that members on all sides of the house are disappointed that the government has not seen fit to increase the exemptions granted people in the low income brackets for 1946, and are dissatisfied with the amount of increase for 1947.
The Minister of Finance, when he spoke on the question, realized I think that the government's proposals would not meet with the approval of the people of Canada, because he went to some length .to try to justify the government's actions in this regard. I should like to quote what he had to say as reported at page 2914 of Hansard:
I am aware of suggestions, made by persons who may not be familiar with all the facts, that the exemption limits be raised to $1,000 for single persons and $2,000 for married, or even to $1,200 and $2,400. We have carefully examined these and other suggestions and have come to the conclusion that exemptions of $750 and $1,500 are as high as can be reasonably proposed under present circumstances.
In the first place, we must still raise very large amounts of revenue. Even if no tax reductions were made, our revenues will fall considerably short of our expenditures and far short of our total financial requirements for the current year. Moreover, as I have outlined, there is already a great excess of purchasing power and we must not add unnecessarily to it.
Secondly, we are all, I believe, agreed that the income tax is the fairest and best tax on which to rely for the bulk of our revenue. More than any other, it takes ability to pay properly into account. We must, I consider, rely upon it as heavily as we can, subject to the limits imposed by its effects on incentive and efficiency. This applies as well in the lower brackets as in the higher, We cannot secure proper equity and fair treatment if the exemptions from income tax are so high as to exclude most of those receiving incomes.
There are three points which I wish to deal with in this regard. The minister says, first, that we would not be justified in exempting this class from taxation; second, that we could not expand demand at this time owing to the shortage of'goods; and third, that to increase exemptions, as proposed by various organizations, would bring about a serious loss of revenue.
Dealing with the first of these points, I would remind the government that during the war when they were continually asking the people to make great sacrifices and to accept

the burdens of total war, they held before the people the hope that after the war the government would introduce a new social order. As a matter of fact they went beyond that, because the Prime Minister said that unless this new social order was well on the way before the end of the war we might look for it in vain. Several times during the war we in this group reminded the government that similar statements had been made repeatedly during the war of 1914-19. The government spokesman assured us, however, that the situation to-day was entirely different, that we could not compare conditions in this war with conditions in the last one, because we had now expanded production to the point where we could give everyone a decent standard of living.
I think the people are beginning to realize that the new social order is drifting further and further away instead of coming nearer. We must realize that we cannot hope to attain that order by following in the ruts of the past. If we are to attain it we shall have to blaze a new trail or we shall become bogged down as we were between the two wars.
The Minister of Finance, when he spoke, compared our exemptions with those given by other countries, and I admit that the comparison was quite favourable. But I think he overlooks one important point. The people of this country are not interested in what exemptions are allowed in other countries; they are interested only in what exemptions can be given here. Therefore the first important point for us to consider is whether or not these exemptions can at this time be raised higher than they are; and the second point is, would such a policy benefit not merely the people who are exempted from taxation but the people of Canada as a whole.
I do not think there is any doubt that the answer to both questions must be in the affirmative. First of all, in considering the question it is well to remember that we in Canada are blest with more resources per capita than the people of the great majority of other countries. We have an income of around Sll billion, which means an average of 83,000 for a family of four. The first step to be taken in any new social order should be, therefore, to raise the standard of living of people in the low income group. We should attempt to establish a minimum standard of $1,200 for single persons and $2,000 for married people.
To come back to the question, would exempting these low income groups benefit Canada as a whole, the minister will agree that the most important problem before us at the present time is to expand production as

Income War Tax
rapidly as possible, especially the production of consumer good9 so that we may have at all times a brimming pool of consumer goods from whidh the people may draw. I would say that one of the logical ways to help maintain production would be to maintain a contented people. The minister will agree that the high rates of taxation to-day are causing wide discontent among the workers of the country. One of the best ways to prove to them that we are really sincere in this matter is to bring about a substantial reduction of taxation to the people in the low income groups, thereby ensuring that they will be able to have a better standard of living in the future.
The next point of the minister was that we must not expand demand at this time because we already have a large volume of purchasing power in circulation. While it is true there is no actual lack of demand on balance to-day, largely owing to the fact that we have an accumulation of war savings and that large benefits are being paid out to the men of the armed services, nevertheless we must not forget that there are in Canada to-day many people in t'he low income groups who have no savings. I am well aware of the fact that some people will say that they Should have. They charge that had these people saved during the war they would now have savings. Bu't let us not forget that before the war many in this group were unemployed and probably on the relief rolls, thereby enduring a standard of living far below that which anybody should be asked to exist on; they were persons who had to do without things which most of us would consider to be absolutely essential. Within a year or two after the war started these people were able to jet a job, but even after they obtained jobs there were so many things they required that they were not in a position to save much; and just about the time that they might have been able to save something the government brought about the heavy increase in taxation in 1942. Therefore they were not in a position to accumulate savings.
However, if the minister is going to argiue that to increase exemptions at this time to $1,200 for single persons and $2,000 for married people will be inflationary, then I would remind him of what the leader of this group the hon. member for Peace River, suggested when he spoke. He suggested that we Should give to such persons tax bonds in return for the money obtained from them; in other words, that we should adopt a policy of deferred tax remissions for those in the low income groups. On several occasions during the war I emphasized the need for compulsory
savings. I pointed out that we were accumulating a large amount of debt claims. I know that during the war people sought to soft pedal the idea that the national debt would do the country any harm. As a matter of fact many said that in reality a national debt was a national asset, because everybody who had a share in it would be receiving interest, and therefore so long as the debt was owned internally there was nothing to be concerned about. That would have been true if the national debt had been distributed equitably amongst the people so that all the people would have had a claim against the debt or asset if you like to call it that. But unfortunately during the war the method of financing did not help to bring about an equitable distribution of the debt. I should like to remind the minister that during the war loan campaigns we generally found that approximately one-third of one per cent of the subscribers purchased sixty per cent of the total subscriptions, thereby bringing about an inequitable distribution. However, if at that time our proposals had been accepted whereby persons in the low income groups would have not paid any taxes but merely accumulated compulsory savings, then they too would 'have 'had a claim against those accumulated debt claims. Then at the end of the war, just as soon as production had increased to the point where it could take care of the demands of the people, the compulsory savings could -have been paid back to them, and in that way those in the low income groups would have been able to share in the benefits of expanded production at the end of the war.
Sudh a policy of deferred tax remissions or tax bonds instead of taxation would have been a partial insurance against a depression in the future. In that regard I Should like to quote from a speech made on October 7, 1942, at Montebello, by the deputy minister of finance, Doctor Clark, which reads as follows:
The same philosophy which has led to these very high taxes in yvar time is likely to dictate a reversal of that policy in the post-war years. To-day, demand is far in excess of supply. Consumer purchasing power is far in excess of the available supply of consumer goods and services. The taxing authorities therefore must, through high taxes, syphon off as much as possible of that surplus purchasing power if we are to avoid all the evils of inflation. On the other hand the post-war period is likely to pose ah entirely different set of conditions. If we may judge by the record of the past, we are likely to see, after a temporary period of dislocation and hesitation followed possibly by a consumer goods purchasing boom, a period during which unless the state acts aggressively and intelli-

gently to prevent it, supply or potential supply may tend to be far in excess of effective demand.
What will then be needed is to safeguard against deflation, not to prevent inflation. If we are to avoid a long depression and mass unemployment, the policy required will be one of stimulation of the economy, one that will create expansionist tendencies, one that will provide incentives to expansion of production, one that will encourage the consumer to spend and expand his purchasing power. In short, one which will keep the national income from falling to abnormally low levels.
In his report of 1946, the governor of the Bank of Canada emphasized exactly the same point and said that in a few years our major problem will be to maintain an effective demand against the production of the country. Therefore, as I say, one method of helping to insure against lack of effective demand in the future will be to build up a reserve of purchasing power in the hands of those who are in the low income groups. Building up large reserves of purchasing power in the hands of those who are already well-off will not be any guarantee against lack of effective demand, because these people are already spending the money to buy the goods they require. On the other hand, those in the low income groups will not be in a position to spend unless they have a reserve of purchasing power. Such a reserve of purchasing power can be built up by the remission of taxes to the people.
The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply has suggested that a shelf of national projects should be built up to take care of the situation. I will agree that in part it may help to meet the situation. Building up a reserve of purchasing power by remission of taxes would also help to take care of a depression.
At this time I should like to emphasize the fact that, in the final analysis, in order to guarantee that this country may run on an even course without depression we shall finally have to come to the proposals which this group has made from time to time; that we shall guarantee to the people a minimum standard of living up to the full capacity of the country to supply by the payment of consumer credits directly to the consumer.
Once or twice the minister has twitted us on the point that during the war he has not heard much about social credit. Of course the reason is obvious. The purpose of social credit is to distribute surpluses. In war time, owing to the demands of war there are no surpluses to distribute, but from now on I can assure the committee that it will be hearing more and more on this point, because as our problems increase social credit is the only solution.
The last objection of the minister to raising exemptions was that it would cause a loss of revenue to the government. In that regard I 
should like to quote the minister's own words, to be found at page 3589 of Hansard:
So we are brought back to this, whether we like it or not and whether or not it is popular; we are brought back to the necessity of equating revenue and expenditures when we have high employment and a high national income.
Earlier he had said:	.
This question was raised by the financial critic of the opposition in the opening speech, when he asked: "Do we or do we not believe in deficit budgeting?" Well, Mr. Speaker, I must say I cannot see how a responsible government or a responsible minister of finance could possibly advocate a system of continued deficits in the Dominion of Canada, that is, deficits year after year, year after year.
First, I might refer to a speech made by the chairman of the advisory committee on reconstruction, in 1943, which appears at page 29 of the proceedings of the senate committee on economic reestablishment and social security. He was speaking of the need for national projects after the war, and it is interesting to note what he has to say on this question raised by the minister, in regard to lack of revenue:
I wanted to add one further point there, namely, that the recognition of that policy of public investment as a marginal factor to take up the slack of private investment at any period implies the necessity of a complete change in our budget philosophy. We should still have an annual budget for probable revenues and expenditures; but so far as public investment expenditures are concerned for the construction of all kinds of projects, it would obviously be necessary to have a budget which extends over a period of years. Mr. Churchill two Sundays ago suggested four years as the period for a plan. That may be perfectly right, politically thinking, but economically I prefer a period of seven or ten years. It may also be true-I mention this because somebody may think of it-that the adoption of that policy will mean a slight but continuous increase in the total public debt of Canada over the next hundred years.
In other words he suggested we would require to have unbalanced budgets for the next hundred years. My only observation in that connection is, why stop there; why not admit that you are bound) to go into debt year after year, as long as you continue under the present system? You have only to look to the past to see that since confederation we have had only fifteen balanced budgets, in a period of seventy-eight years, and to realize that we shall probably be doing the same thing in future. If we could not have balanced budgets when the national debt was only two or three billion dollars, is it likely that we shall have balanced budgets when the debt has increased to around sixteen billion dollars? No. My point is that even in the years when we had a balanced federal budget the public debt increased. For instance,

Income War Tax
from 1924 to 1929 we had balanced budgets, and the national debt decreased by $250,000,000. But the debt of the provinces increased by over $500,000,000, so that even in that period the public debt increased by over $250,000,000. Really what we did was this. By this government forcing the provinces to accept responsibility for certain payments it balanced its own budget but forced the provinces into debt. If it is a question as between the provinces or the dominion going into debt, I should say it would be far better for the dominion to do so because it has access to certain types of funds which are not available to the provinces; or, as we say, it can use national money and avoid going into debt in any shape or form.
The interesting point in the minister's speech was his statement that we must attempt to have a balanced budget. Just to show how much faith we can have in that proposal, I would suggest to the committee that we read What he said in September, 1939, in regai d to the financing of the war, and see how far short, he fell in carrying out that policy. Then have we any reason to believe he will be able to fulfil his promise in that regard in future? This is what he said in the budget speech of September 12, 1939, at page 140 of Hansard'.
All this is not to say that a small and carefully regulated amount of credit expansion may not be desirable in the early stages of the war in order to assist the increase of production and employment . . . However, as soon as the expansion of employment and production gets well under wajr and certainly before it approaches its limits, further expansion of the supply of money and credit must be stopped if the danger of progressive inflation is to be avoided.
When did the minister follow that policy? Just as soon as we had reached the position of full employment and high production, the minister said there should be no further credit expansion. In 1943, 1944 and 1945 we bad a high level of employment and a high income; yet in each of those years we had an expansion of credit to the extent of hundreds of millions of dollars. The reason is, of course, obvious, and I shall deal with that later on. In spite of the heavy taxation and large borrowings from the people, the government still lacked funds to meet its expenditures. In the last year of the war, 1945, the deficit was around one and three-quarter billion. How did we make up those deficits? Partly, as I say, by borrowing the savings of the people, and partly by the creation of new money. We borrowed from the chartered banks something in the neighbourhood of $3,000 million in new money. W'hy was that done? The minister knows the reason. We borrowed that money from the 63260-240
banks in order to maintain a maximum war effort. The Prime Minister promised the people time and again that no financial restrictions would be allowed to impede the war effort. If the people had been familiar with the social credit proposals they would have seen that even in war time it would be necessary to have the creation of money. I say the reason is obvious. We have emphasized the fact that owing to certain practices which are inherent within the system, industry can not maintain an effective demand against its own production; that is to say, it does not distribute sufficient purchasing power to maintain a demand against the goods it produces. That is in peace time. Then in war time the government became the greatest purchaser of goods and material in the country; and in spite of the fact that they taxed the people just as far as they dared tax them, in spite of the fact that they borrowed all the savings of the people that they dared borrow, still they were not able to get, enough money to buy the goods and services they required. Therefore, in order to make up that deficiency in their purchasing power, they had to create in the neighbourhood of $3,000 million during the war.
One of the main purposes of taxation during the war was to curtail spending, because fifty per cent of our production was going for war purposes. To-day the war is over and the total production of the country is once more available to the people. Therefore, as Doctor Clark suggests, in the very near future we shall have to bring about a considerable reduction in, taxation in order to maintain an effective demand against our production. In his book entitled "The World Crisis," Mr. Churchill warned of the aftermath of the war. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario began to quote it the other day but did1 not read the full paragraph, and I should like to put the whole statement on record. Referring to 'armistice day, November 11, 1918, which concluded ithe first war, Mr. Churchill said:
A requisition for half a million houses would not have seemed more difficult to comply with than those we were already in process of executing for 100,000 aeroplanes, or 20,000 guns, oi two million tons of projectiles. But a new set of conditions began to rule from 11 o'clock onward. The money cost, which had never been considered by us to be a factor capable of limiting the supply of the armies, asserted a claim to priority from the moment the fighting stopped.
It is sometimes surprising the way history seems to repeat itself. During the discussion on the health estimates the Minister of National Health and Welfare began the same old srtory all over again. When we were

Income War Tax

discussing old age pensions, advocating a pension of $50 a month at the age of sixty, the Minister of National Health and Welfare told us it would be impossible to do this because it would cost too much money and that- the government did not have the money. When an hon. member from this group suggested that national money could be used, the minister once again returned to the old story about turning the printing presses loose. I am surprised that the minister should insult the intelligence of hon. members by such an asinine remark, because, as I have said, during the war when we wanted to expand the war effort of the country we did) not hesitate to create $3 billion in new money for that purpose. When we created that $3 billion of new money, did we turn the printing presses loose? The government knows very well we did not. It is true that there was an increase in the amount of dominion notes. We increased them to the extent necessary to satisfy the requirements of the people in that regard. That was only a small percentage of the total amount of money issued. During the war did we ever hear the Minister of Finance say that we could not have tanks, ships or aeroplanes because no money was available? One thing and one thing only was taken into Consideration in connection with the war effort, and that was: What are our material resources? So long as we had the men and materials available there was no suggestion that we could not have ships, tanks and aeroplanes because we had not the money to pay for them.
To the extent that a fair and equitable system of taxation fails to meet government expenditures, national money must be created. Otherwise we are bound to have an expanding debt, as was suggested by Doctor James, chairman of the reconstruction committee advising the government. In the past we have urged that national money should be used by the government to make up the deficiency in revenue. In the past it was argued by the Minister of Finance that national money would be more inflationary than money issued by the chartered banks. I do not think the Minister of Finance would argue that to-day, because I know the officials of the Bank of Canada will not argue it. They take the stand that they are thoroughly capable of controlling the aetiqns of the chartered banks, even though national money is issued.
