I shall conclude my remarks by summarizing what I have already said. The greatest need to-day is an expansion of production to meet demands. One of the greatest obstacles to such expansion is the high taxation of low incomes, because it causes discontent among the workers. As pointed out by Doctor Clark and the governor of the Bank of Canada, one of the greatest dangers in a few years will be the lack of demand for goods produced. Therefore we urge that in order to restrict demand now and to provide for a reserve of purchasing power later, tax bonds should be issued to people in low income brackets, instead of imposing taxation upon them. Then, to offset loss of revenue, national money should be used. There would be no danger of inflation, because money would be issued only to balance demand with supply. Therefore we in this group urge that the exemptions for single persons be raised to $1,200 and for married persons to $2,000.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to speak on taxation and on the gold mines of my constituency, in order to inform the government, in a spirit of co-operation, of the views of my constituents.
As everyone knows, the mines of Northwestern Quebec, more than anywhere else in the country, have been adversely affected by the decision to establish the parity of the Canadian dollar with the American dollar. Our mines have thereby lost a 10 per cent, premium and the price of gold fell from $38.50 to $35 per ounce. I have heard the opposition voice destructive criticism, inasmuch as they were attacking the masterpiece of the present government, its fight against inflation which has been successful up to now. In view of the tremendous increase in prices of goods in other countries, and even

Income. War Tax
in the United States, it is not necessary to expound lengthy theories to show the efficient administration and the foresight of our ministers, and especially the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley).
Mr. Chairman, the people benefit by the maintenance of prices at a low level and, as usual, our government has taken steps in order to protect the people, over the protests of certain financial interests.
I wish therefore, on behalf of my electors, to congratulate the ministers for the fight waged against inflation during the war and during the difficult post-war period. The decision arrived at in regard to the parity of the Canadian dollar seems excellent, inasmuch as it is part of a series of measures necessary to control inflation. However, I deem it my duty to acquaint the government with certain disastrous results of this decision, in order to suggest new remedial measures not with a view to eliminate what has already been done but to supplement it.
The decision in regard to the parity of the dollar has affected the gold mines of northwestern Quebec especially in two different ways:
First, if gold sells for only $35 per ounce, those mines operating on a small margin of profit, and especially those having low grade ore, will show' a deficit, and will have to close down, particularly now that the prices of materials have increased and that they are facing demands for higher wages on the part of their employees. Other mines that may continue their operations will be forced to leave underground a large quantity of gold which they cannot mine profitably with gold selling for $35 per ounce but which they could extract when the price was $38.50 per ounce. Mr. 'Chairman, I wish to draw the attention of the government to the enormous loss of gold which will result.
Second, it has taken away the confidence of the public in our gold mines. The stock market went down to a point which we had not known for several years. Unless some countermeasure is taken immediately to remedy the situation, mines in the stage of promotion will be abandoned. I must draw the government's attention to the fact that all gold or base metal mines now in operation had to be promoted and without the help of the public who, in the early stages, had the courage and far sightedness to take risks inherent in all mining venture, Canada would now be a small country deprived of its mining industry, which is essential to its economy. If we force companies in promotion out of business, we shall deprive Canada of its future mining industry.

We must therefore ensure a reasonable profit to producers whose working expenses are out of proportion with the value of their production, and to mines being promoted so that they may one day operate. In addition, in ensuring the development of this industry, we must help prospectors in finding purchasers for those mine fields because, according to Mr. Dumulon, Chairman of the North Western Quebec Prospectors Association, they have been badly hit by the decision regarding the parity of the dollar.
I wish to insist on the fact that no commercial enterprise has any chance of success unless the profits are proportioned to the risks taken by the investors. There are exceptionally great risks in the mining industry and they must therefore be balanced by exceptionally large profits for those few who have the chance of succeeding. I wish to mention the report of the Senate's Natural Resources Committee where it is stated that, in the Province of Ontario, only one half of one per cent of all mining enterprises are successful. I also wish to refer to the statistics submitted to the said committee by the Western Quebec Mining Association, showing that the income on the average investments in mines, when the mining enterprise is successful, is not more profitable than investments in government securities at 3 per cent.

I am surprised to see this section 21(b) in the budget resolutions in this form. The government is legislating, as to income tax, not for this year but for 1947 and subsequent years. I come from a city which is now paying nearly one-third of all the cash income taxes paid in the dominion, and I object to this way of doing things. During the war we were promised two things. At that time the people were taxed to death and controlled to death, and now, fifteen months after the war, they are more taxed and more controlled than ever-so much so that we are on the verge of becoming a straight socialist state. Taxation is driving many of the small business men of this country out of business Just look at the paltry deductions allowed- only $300, $100, $300.
Two years ago family allowances running into hundreds of millions of dollars were introduced. We should consider the case of those who became ill. Take the working classes in your constituency, Mr. Chairman, or in the constituencies of Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton or Vancouver; how often the working people in those districts take ill and find that their doctors cannot get them into the hospitals or cannot get them any nurses or domestic help during the period of illness. They closed down two of the largest floors at Toronto general hospital-no nurses. The splendid Victorian Order of Nurses go around to the homes of the working classes for $2.50 a week but the sick get no help from the government in the way of deduction allowances. In many cases they have to borrow money from anybody they know. Any member of parliament knows that. There are

Income War Tax
hardly any nurses, but they have what they call practical nurses. I have five or six letters on this matter from my constituents. I wrote the wartime prices and trade board, and the secretary in reply informed me that there are no regulations with respect to nurses. I may say that the Quebec legislature has done something; it has decided that if nurses are to charge 86 a day they should have other capacities and qualifications than being able to help in the house, they must have a certificate from some hospital.
People are taxed and controlled to death, and they cannot get the services they need. If they need to get into a hospital there are no vacancies. Since the war was over, a year ago, a considerable body of workers in the industrial centres have remained in the cities and want to stay there, but they cannot find a place to live, and there is an extraordinary number of cases of evictions before the county court judges. I was talking to one of the judges last Sunday, and he told me about some people who were to be evicted, with no place to go.
The present high tax levels disastrously affect, with practically no deductions, all classes of our people. It was reported that the Minister of National Revenue made some promises in this direction, and though he denied that he said it, if he did not say it, others did. I have heard it in the Toronto district; I have read of it in the newspapers. I accept the word of the minister, but the fact remains that the statement attributed to him was publicized all over our city by the Globe and the Star. They made big headlines about it.
Our people were promised a year ago, after the war, "death to controls". Now they are controlled and taxed to death. Consider the position of the working man who has to pay $6 a day to a so-called practical nurse who may not know enough to give an injection. The law in Quebec is better than that, and I believe there should be a dominion-wide law requiring that a nurse must be qualified when required in the home. Enough qualified nurses are not available.
We are now legislating for 1947. The government did the same thing before, and then, when the year arrived that they were going to reduce taxes they changed the schedules around. The book of statistics with the green cover in the possession of my hon. friend contains a lot of statistics and we now have the new schedules for 1947, which is a matter for next year's ways and means committee. What we are doing now is just wasting our time; we have talked all day and have passed only one section; the second section, paragraph (b) is still before us.
I suggest that some protection be provided by deductions for the ordinary working man who has to get a nurse once in a while, and that some further allowance should be made. A reduction equivalent to only $300 is not enough; it would not last a week where a patient's condition is serious and getting worse. I know the case of a man in my constituency, where the doctor insisted that he get another practical nurse; one will not do to-day; he has to get two, at $6 a day, plus room, and meals must be provided as well. I sent his letter to the wartime prices and trade board. I hear now that another temporary nurse is wanted; and the man simply has to borrow money.
I do not know where all this is going to end. The other day in the reading room I was looking at one of our papers in which a plea was made for cash: everybody wants cash; especially the government wants cash to carry on the business of the country. To my mind there should be a halt. If we are to legislate for 1946 let us legislate for 1946 and pass the ways and means resolutions. Do not be tinkering with the supposed requirements of 1947 and the following year. The government may not be here then. The way they are carrying on now they probably will not be; since at times we are having some close votes.
I venture to say that the right hon. and learned member who is the leader of the house-an estimable gentleman-could himself give some information as to the extent that people in the city he so honourably represents are complaining about the same matters. I appreciate what the government has done in the sphere of family allowances, but when you pass all this you will have to go over the same story when 1947 comes. I urge that some additional allowance be made in these deductions for especially urgent, important and extraordinary cases such as I have suggested.
The hon. member for Temiscouata made a forty-minute speech this morning on the resolution. The other day one of the newspapers, noting that he and I sit at opposite ends of the chamber, called us "those two inimitable end-men" as if we were in a minstrel show. I am not going to imitate the other end-man to-day by making a forty-minute speech to hold the line, so that I have confined my remarks to four or five minutes; but I would conclude by pointing out that there is general complaint that it is impossible to get nurses or any kind of help, and that the deduction amounts to practically nothing; it might just as well be wiped out, What is the use of talking about $300? That does not pay nurses and medicine for one

I desire to do so because I have received many letters and telegrams of one kind and another from individuals and organizations requesting that I support them in their demand for exemptions from income tax to the extent of $1,200 for single persons and $2,000 for married persons. I desire to do so now. I dc not know that I am going to discuss or to recommend to the minister how he should readjust the tax structure to

make this possible, because I realize that the present administration is working within the confines of certain financial rules and, I do not care what party it is, working within the confines of those rules they will never be able to alleviate the tremendous burdens of taxation that now rest upon the people. With our huge debt and expenditures the rules will not permit them to do it, and until they change the rules, the people must know that for generations to come, for ever and a day, they will be burdened with heavy loads of taxation.
I should like to ask the minister just what starting point the government uses to determine the exemptions the people of Canada should get from taxation. If my guess is right, and I think it is, they start somewhat in this fashion. They outline their year's programme. They say: We are going to do this, and we are going to do that, and it is going to cost us so much money; therefore we shall have to get that amount of money from some source; if we are to get that money from somewhere we must devise ways and means of getting it, and we have only one way of getting it, namely, to tax it out of the people. That seems to be the government's starting point. But what should be the proper starting point? It should be something like this. They should calculate what is a reasonably good standard of living for every individual, whether he be a single or a married man, and then say; We will refuse to tax anyone who does not come up to that reasonably good standard of living.

I can tell the minister how he can get a nice little pile of money, and he will be doing a great service to the country. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Would the hon. member try to relate his remarks a little more closely to the resolution under discussion?

Yes; thank you for reminding me, Mr. Chairman. The questions which were asked me took me off the resolution.
I was discussing exemptions to the extent of $750 for single and $1,500 for married people.
I should like the minister to be able to tell us when on earth he expects to do away with such tremendous burdens of taxation as we have. We are paying $481 million a year to service the debt of Canada alone. Even though we did not go into debt another dollar, the people of Canada would have to turn out their pockets and pay $481 million a year. I shoiild like the minister to tell us when we can expect higher exemptions and less taxation and at the same time meet the interest on that debt alone, without incurring another dollar of debt. I should like any other party to tell me the same thing. I declare to you, Mr. Chairman, that it cannot be done within the confines of the rules of the present debttaxing game of finance. If it can be done, I want him to tell me how. It is time the people of Canada became aware of the fact that it cannot be done just so long as governments insist on financing by debt-taxation finance.

I can answer that last question asked by the hon. member for Macleod. As hon. members know, I have been worried considerably especially since I left my parliament in session; I have not even prorogued it. In fact this whole debt problem has been of great concern to me, so much so that I actually went off my feed, as it were-lost my appetite. However, I made up my mind that I would go down to the hotel and get a lobster supper. Whether it was the result of this lobster supper or not, I am not sure, but during the night I had a vision, and I was able quite easily to solve the problem of all these debts. Whether it was the Angel Gabriel I saw standing in the dark doorway of my bedchamber, or whether it was the landlady in her nightie coming to see if I was ill, or whether it was natural for me to gurgle and rumble my tonsils in peaceful slumber, I shall never know. But it did occur to me, how can we solve this terrific problem of debt? Hon. members know that I am interested in the lowly pig; they also know that I am interested in that great and strenuous art of sheep shearing, but they did not know that I was interested in horses. One horse that I was always interested in was one owned by a fellow named Trojan. Since I was a little boy I always wondered what breed the Trojan horse was. I determined to find out, and indirectly I learned how to solve this debt problem. I was disappointed in the horse. When I went to find out what it was,
I learned that it was nothing but a hammerheaded, broken-winded, raw-boned, switchtailed, old Temiscouata pacing mare. On the other hand, Trojan was the very man for our next prime minister. My hopes rose immediately and then, fell when I learned that the poor fellow was dead; in fact, he had been dead for approximately two thousand years.
Two delegations waited upon Trojan. The first consisted of the minister of finance, the deputy minister of finance, the assistant to the deputy minister of finance and the assistant to the assistant to the deputy minister of finance, the deputy minister of taxation, the assistant deputy minister of taxation and the assistant to the assistant deputy minister of taxation, and two stenographers. They were not the kind of stenographers some hon. members are thinking of, but they did have this in common; they wore no stockings. These two stenographers were just a couple of elderly gentlemen, knock-kneed, bare-legged and baldheaded, with a saddle blanket thrown over one shoulder and loosely tied about the middle and a string of poplar leaves tied around their heads, carrying a great bundle of papyrus

Income War Tax
which they called the budget. They presented to Trojan the records of all the debts that had accumulated during the wars, which amounted to what were tremendous sums in those days. They also complained about the old soldiers of the Trojan wars, the old soldier settlers, and asked, "How in the world can we get them to pay up what they owe?" "Well," Trojan said, " What have you done?" " Well, we have taxed the people. We have foreclosed on homes, farms and factories. We have brought them to their knees and some of them we have under lock and key." " In prison? " asked Trojan. "Oh, no; we have them in insane asylums. We have driven some of them crazy." Well, Trojan just got up and went into the kitchen to get a great meat cleaver, whereupon the suspicious delegation went out through the window.
The next delegation to wait on him consisted of three old soldier settlers of the Trojan wars, worn, weary and haggard, who presented their case. Trojan placed his hand on their shoulders and gave them three pieces of silver, telling them to go to Jones' meat market and buy up all the wieners on sale. Next he sent for the records of all the debts, had them piled in the market place, set fire to them and had a wiener roast. That was two thousand years ago.

I thought I was on paragraph 2; I thought this had to do with taxation and methods of getting rid of it. What I have said is perfectly true; hon. members can go to the library and find out for themselves that this actually took place. When these debts accumulated in those days they were just, burned. Nobody cried about it except the deputy ministers concerned, and everyone knew they were just crocodile tears which soon dried up. Nothing more was said about it from that day to this. There is the solution to this debt problem.

speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
3.	That for the 1947 and subsequent taxation years the deduction of $1,500 from the income of a married person be reduced,
(a)	where the spouse has an income of more than $250 and less than $750 by the amount by which the spouse's income is more than $250, or
(b)	where the spouse has an income of more than $750, to $750.
whether or not the wife's income is earned income.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Following the practice when we began perhaps I might give a brief explanation of the legislation which is to be founded upon this resolution. The effect of the legislation to follow this resolution is to return to the basis of taxation for husband and wife each having an income in excess of S750 to the pre^l942 position, and also to provide for a reduction in the exemption granted to the husband when the wife has an income in excess of S250 but below the exemption limit.
Prior to 1942 the law provided that when husband and wife each had taxable incomes the husband lost the exemption granted a married person, and he and his wife were taxed individually as single persons. As a temporary measure to encourage married women to enter war work during the acute period of labour shortage the law was amended in 1942 to allow the husband to retain the married exemption when, his wife had a taxable income derived from employment. The proposal under the resolution we are now considering is that from 1947 onward this special exemption will be withdrawn in order to place their' position on a more equitable basis in relation to other taxpayers.
A further change proposed for married couples where the wife has an income below the taxable limits also removes in a large degree a privileged position previously enjoyed by married taxpayers. Under the present law a married man would be allowed to claim the full 81,500 exemption granted because of his wife's dependence on him, and at the same time the wife could have an income up to $750 completely exempt from tax, so that together they would have a combined exemption of $2,250 compared with a total exemption of only $1,500 granted to two single persons having the same income, or to married persons, the wife having no separate income. To remove a substantial part of this advantage we are proposing that when the wife has an income of more than $250 but less than $750 the husband's exemption will be reduced by the amount by which his wife's income exceeds $250. In effect a husband will be given full married exemption when his wife's income does not exceed $250 a year. When the wife's income exceeds this amount the $1,500 allowance given the husband is reduced in proportion to the excess of her income over $250.
In connection with this proposal I might perhaps point out to the committee that under the federal income tax in the United States a husband may claim full married exemption only if he includes all his wife's income with his own, which of course is more restrictive than the proposal contained in this resolution; and also that in the United Kingdom a husband and wife living together are compel-

Income War Tax

led to file a joint return, though I am advised the husband is allowed a small deduction in respect of his wife's earned income.

The minister said a married man would have an exemption. I know of married couples where the man is a cripple and unable to work, and the wife earns the money. In that case she would have the exemption, would she?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: This applies to the same extent to whichever consort has the income. I am sorry; I should have made that clear.

I had some remarks to make on this section in the budget debate. To my mind it is one of the most foolish provisions of the present budget. I do not often use such strong words in this house, but certainly this resolution will have the effect of withdrawing from the labour supply of the country a great many married women who are in a position to render valuable service. Without doubt it will cut down the service they will give. If I were interested in the theory of taxation and were to do everything according to the book of rules, with little regard to the effect on humanity or on the economic welfare of the nation or on inflation or on production, probably I would do what the minister is suggesting under this resolution. Undoubtedly it is fair and equitable; if a man's wife is working and earning more than S750, then the husband should not be entitled to the marital exemption because both parties are bringing in income. But let us stop right there. What would be the effect of this new provision concerning earnings over S250, which is not a very large amount for a married woman? It will mean that married women without family responsibilities, whose children are grown up or who have not been blessed with children and who work during part of the year, for instance women who might have been domestics or who might do some nursing for thirty or forty or fifty per cent of the ordinary working year, soon find that their annual income exceeds S250. If it does, this provision immediately comes into effect, reducing the husband's income.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Reducing the husband's
exemption.

Thank you; reducing the husband's exemption, which means that he pays more taxes. This discourages the wife from doing further work, and I am sure it will have a direct and immediate effect. There are also many women who work along with their husbands, as in the needle trades. The work is taken from the shop to the home, and the wife receives part of the income. But she

very quickly gets an amount larger than $250. I have had a number of letters in this regard from my own riding, and I know that it will apply not only to the needle trades and to domestic services, but also to the nursing profession and many other activities which hon. members may call to mind for themselves.
When he presented his budget the Minister of Finance stated that tlhe most important thing, from the point of view of running the economic affairs of the country to-day, was production; and if there was one thing the budget should make possible it was greater production-not only because production in itself is essential if we are to have a higher standard of living, realizing as we do that we can improve it only if we produce more goods and services, but because we are faced with the grave danger of inflation. Inflation is simply a condition caused by more money than goods available at prevailing price levels. If we want to help defeat this disaster of inflation which we are facing in a very real way, then the more goods and services we produce the greater is the tendency to defeat it. I do not say it will be completely defeated, but the minister has certainly gone on record as saying it w'omld be a help. I think most economists will agree that the more we can produce, the less likely we are to have a serious increase in prices. So while I agree with the minister that there is a certain fairness in this resolution, I believe this is the wrong time to change this part of the act from the way it stood during the war, the way it stands on the books to-day.
The budget is directed to increased production, but now we are asked to come back to a consideration of fairness as the predominant motive. I offer the suggestion to the committee-I hope it will be considered seriously-that this provision is one which should be on the statute book at one stage in a business cycle, and not at another stage. If there are more jobs than people to take them, then we should encourage married women to vTork, even though there might be a slight element of unfairness. It is not very great. It is almost a dog-in-the-manger attitude to take with regard to married persons both of whom are working. It is not a serious inequality. When, there are more workers than jobs available I would put in this restrictive measure. It is restrictive to production, perhaps, but it does help provide work, and it means that instead of two in a family working there will be a greater tendency for only one to work. Therefore I suggest to the acting minister and the committee that the resolution be changed so

Income War Tax
that at the present time we put the emphasis on, production, and at some later time we might put the emphasis on fairness.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The general rule is found
in section 6(1) of the Income War Tax Act, which states:
In computing the amount of the profits or gains to be assessed, a deduction shall not be allowed in respect of
(a) disbursements or expenses not wholly, exclusively and necessarily laid out or expended for the purpose of earning the income.
Then follow a number of other paragraphs relating to depreciation and the like. A corporation or any taxpayer is entitled to deduct from his gross income expenses which are wholly, exclusively and necessarily laid out or expended for the purpose of earning the income. That is the general criterion. Therefore the test must be whether the expenditure for advertising comes within that description; whether , the travelling expenses of a commercial traveller, or a company officer or executive, or the employee of a company, come within that general description. This of course is administered by the Department of National Revenue. The taxpayer's accounts are examined to see whether the expenses claimed as deductions are properly claimed having regard to the provisions of the section I have just quoted.

I would presume, then, that the minister provides some limits within which these expenses are chargeable. For example, surely he lays down a maximum which any corporation may charge for advertising, or a maximum percentage of income which will be allowable for travelling expenses or for the entertainment of convention delegates. Is it within the prerogative of an official in the income tax branch to set, according to his own judgment, what the limits would be? It

would seem to me that a corporation could argue reasonably successfully that political contributions, for example, were a legitimate business expense if they had reason to believe that the corporation would be benefited by such contributions.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No such claim would be allowed. It would not be a legitimate advertising expense and would not come within the provisions of the section, I quoted.
I have reason to believe that such contributions have been claimed successfully as deductions.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They should be brought to the attention of the tax department. I am sure they will see that the situation is corrected.
The minister states that contributions of that type for political purposes are definitely not proper deductions?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I state that without hesitation; there is no question about it at all. Section 6, subsection 2 reads:
The minister may disallow any expense which he in his discretion may determine to be in excess of what is reasonable or normal for the business carried on by the taxpayer, or which was incurred in respect of any transaction or operation which in his opinion has unduly or artificially reduced the income.

As I understand it, the tax collector goes into a firm and checks the advertising account. If more has been spent than was spent in the year before he will ask the reason and perhaps will allow only part.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think that is correct. Hon. members of the committee will appreciate that it is difficult to lay down a definite criterion for all companies. Some types of business require to spend a great deal more for advertising than others. During the war period, when the excess profits tax was in operation- and it still applies-there was a quota set for advertising purposes. Firms were not allowed to exceed an amount based on what they had expended during the base period. I do not want to be held to the exact details as to how the quota was arrived at, but one was set. That has now been discontinued, and the normal procedure is that the taxpayer must show that the advertising expense was incurred and was wholly necessary for the purpose of earning the income. However, that is subject to the control which the minister has under the subsection I have just quoted.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Is the minister aware that communications have gone out to some firms soliciting contributions-I refer in particular to letters over the signature of one Mr. Trestrail, in which he stated that he had reason to be-

lieve that contributions to the kind of thing he was doing would be allowed as a deduction for income tax purposes-which have made this claim?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have no knowledge of the letters sent out by Mr. Trestrail, but I do not know that I would care to accept his interpretation of the income tax law as to what would be or what would not be allowed.
The minister has yet to make a statement on depreciation deductions in connection with plant and equipment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Section 6 provides:
6. (1) In computing the amount of the profits or gains to be assessed, a deduction shall not be allowed in respect of
(n) depreciation, except such amount as the minister in his discretion may allow, including
(i)	such extra depreciation as the minister in his discretion may allow in the case of plant or equipment built or acquired to fulfil orders for war purposes; and

Provided, however, that the minister shall not allow a deduction in respect of depreciation of assets owned by an incorporated taxpayer from the income of the said taxpayer if he is satisfied that the said taxpayer directly or indirectly had or has a controlling interest in a company or companies previously the owner or owners of the said assets or that the said previous owner (which term shall include a series of owners) directly or indirectly had or has a controlling interest in the said taxpayer or that the said taxpayer and the previous owner were or are directly or indirectly subject to the same controlling interest and that the aggregate amount of deductions which have been allowed to the said taxpayer and/or the said previous owner in respect of the depreciation of such assets is equal to or greater than the cost of the said assets to the said previous owner or to the first of the previous owners where more than one.
There are other provisos but I shall not read them all. They were put in a year or two ago to prevent the possibility of undue depreciation being granted. As the committee will appreciate, the minister is given the discretion as to the rates of depreciation. The department has established recognized rates for various types of assets, movable and immovable, which I believe are applied in a uniform fashion to all taxpayers.

I shall have to digest that
statement when I read it on Hansard. It is conceivable that over a number of years an entire plant and its equipment might be written off in the normal income tax practice, but the equipment might still have some value.

Income War Tax
Suppose that a corporation decided to dispose of an obsolete plant which had been written off and which conceivably could be written off according to the regulations. Would the purchase price received be considered as income for that year, or would it be treated as a capital gain which would not concern the income tax department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
If the corporation has had
normal write-offs based on the standard rates-none of this accelerated depreciation to which I have referred-and the plant is sold after it has been completely written off to a stranger, someone who is at arms length, that stranger is entitled to take depreciation on the cost of the property to him.

That is fine for the stranger
who buys, but how about the seller?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It applies to both individuals and corporations.

This obsolete plant has been sold, say for $100,000. What happens to that $100,000 as far as the income tax department is concerned? The plant does not exist but the corporation has had $100,000 of income. Is that considered as current income or as capital gain?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is considered as capital.

It might be a capital
loss.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
A capital loss might exist
in other circumstances. My hon. friend will appreciate that these depreciation rates must be based on the law of averages. For example, if experience proves that machinery is worn out in ten years and a straight line system of depreciation is used, at the end of ten years the machinery would be written off. If some value still remains the owner is fortunate, but it may well happen that the machinery would be worn out and discarded in five years.

The fact is that if your
officials are generous it is by accident only?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
There are standard rates
which are applied to everyone and which, I understand, are based on long experience. I think they are just as close as one can get to what is a really fair rate of depreciation.

With regard to the provisos on page 23 of the Income War Tax Act, as I understand it if a subsequent sale is made and the department is led to assume that its depreciation was too great, it may revise it. Does that work the other way, and would the department assume that it had not been generous enough if a loss occurred?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: As probably my hon. friend knows that provision was inserted several years ago to meet the case of the special accelerated depreciation which was given on the recommendation of the board set up for the purpose of making recommendations in connection with the fulfilling of war contracts. Varying periods of write-off were given, some two years, some three years, some four years. This provision was inserted to provide that if that had proved unduly optimistic the matter could be looked into again. speechtext:
The resolution is, of course, self-explanatory, and provides for an increase in the exemption from $1,500 to $1,800 under the four per cent tax on investment income. The surtax on investment income is and has been, I think, a feature of all income tax systems for some time. In the 1947 budget we are providing for some-fairly substantial -relief to all classes of taxpayers, and in accordance with that principle the exemption for investment income has been raised from $1,500 to $1,800. Some hon. members may suggest that that is insufficient. It is intended, broadly speaking, to give some relief to that large group of small investment income recipients, of widows who are living on inherited income, those to Whom their husbands leave insurance, and that sort of thing, and for that class of person the exemption is raised from $1,500 to $1,800. It does not give any substantial measure of relief to the richer man; I suppose it saves him $12. I am advised that no estimate has been made of what the net cost of this increased exemption
Income War Tax

will be to the treasury, but perhaps I can ask the officials to make such an estimate and give it later on.
It is a step in the right direction, anyway.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: While they are getting these figures-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not guarantee that we can give an exact figure, but we will do the best we can.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: -will they also consider obtaining some estimate as to the number of these people who are the widows that my hon. friend refers to, and how many are the big fellows?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Then I think it was unfair of the minister to use that argument.

speechtext: I do not consider it at all unfair. I think it is perfectly legitimate to say you will exempt investment income up to SI,800 from this four per cent surtax. I think it is perfectly legitimate to use that point, because that as the class it is intended to relieve, and I assure my hon. friend and other members of the committee that it is not intended or designed to relieve the man who has an income of $100,000; it does not make any appreciable difference to him.

I might say that I do not think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre understands this resolution, because the total amount of saving to the taxpayer through increasing the exemption on investment income from 81,500 to $1,800 is four per cent on a difference of $300, namely $12.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I said that.

I think he will realize that if the administration were endeavouring to help anybody they were not trying to help any of his wealthy backers. 6.	That a deduction from tax be allowed in the 1946 and subsequent taxation years to a taxpayer who resides or is ordinarily resident in Canada during only a part of the taxation year of a portion of the tax that would otherwise be payable upon his income during the taxation year that bears the same relation to the whole rax as the period in the taxation year during which he is not resident or ordinarily resident in Canada bears to the whole taxation year.
I desire to say a word or two on this.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have been making a little explanatory statement in respect to each of these clauses, so that perhaps my hon. friend will allow me to do it here. The situation at the moment is that under the charging provisions of the Income Tax Act as it now stands the tax is imposed on the whole income, no matter where derived, of a person resident in Canada at any time in the tax year. Credit is given against the Canadian tax for income tax paid to another country or income derived from sources outside Canada, and in the normal circumstance the credit is sufficient to offset the Canadian tax imposed on the same income. Representations have been made, however, that in some instances there is no credit for foreign taxes because in some countries no income tax is imposed, or else the credit is quite inadequate because of the very low tax in the foreign country. To overcome this objection to the present law, it is proposed that a person resident in Canada for only a part of the year will continue to be taxable on the whole income, but a credit against the Canadian income tax will be allowed based on the proportion which the number of days in which the taxpayer was not a resident of Canada bears to the total number of days in the year. In other words, in effect, under the proposal which is indicated in this resolution a person resident in Canada for a part of the year will pay a Canadian income tax proportionate to the period of residence in Canada.

I have not in mind the particulars of the case with respect to which I now wish to say a word, but a year ago- perhaps the deputy will recall the circumstances-I brought to the attention of the department the case of a gentleman who had been in the United States, working there, who then came back to Canada, and who was bitterly angry over the assessment in this country. Apparently, although he had earned much less in Canada than in the United States, the income tax he paid was very much higher. I have forgotten the exact circumstances of the case, and all I wish to inquire now is as to what the situation is if a man earns $3,000 in the United States and returns to Canada and earns $1,500 or $2,000 in this country. What, will be the relation of the tax payable in Canada to the amount earned in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The answer is this. The tax payable in Canada would be a proportion of the tax on his total income which, in the case which my hon. friend mentions is $4,500. The tax would be calculated on the $4,500 as though that amount had all been earned in Canada, after taking into account the appropriate exemptions. After that result had been arrived at there would be a determination as to how many days he had resided in the United States and how many in Canada. Assuming for the sake of argument that he had spent two-thirds of the time in the United States and one-third in Canada as a resident, the tax payable to Canada would be one-third of the income tax on the $4,500, and presumably he would be taxed on the two-thirds in the United States. The tax would first be computed on his total income for the year, but he would be taxed only in respect of the portion which represented the period during which he resided in this country in that year. I think it would cover the case to which my hon. friend has referred. I remember his bringing it up.

Suppose the tax on the total income of the taxpayer for 1947 is $365 and

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

This resolution, I suggest, has implications that none of us thought of in the first instance. First of all, it ignores the law of domicile. Is it applied to wages as well as to investment income? Let me give an example. A man ordinarily resident in Canada may draw a salary. Can he evade some of his ordinary income tax by going and living in some other country for three months of the year, assuming that he had a job which did not require his continued personal attention here? I could understand it if it were investment income, but even there I would seriously consider whether this was a wise resolution to put into force if the man who takes advantage of it were a domiciled Canadian.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think the answer is this. Under our income tax act, as under the British act, the test for income tax liability has always been residence, not domicile. That has been the principle in our act from its commencement. The United States system is slightly different. Some taxes are imposed on the basis of citizenship and, perhaps, in respect of domicile. I do not know. In any event, under the Canadian and the British law, the main test of liability for income tax has always been residence. Taking the specific case which my hon. friend has cited, if I understood him correctly, an American resident or a domiciled American comes to Canada-

It is the other way around. I am speaking of the domiciled Canadian who has a job here that does not require his personal attention all the year round, and who, for the purpose of evading our somewhat heavy taxation, decides to spend four months of the year in the British West Indies.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
My hon. friend, as a
prominent legal light, knows that residence is a question of fact. It would be a question of. fact whether the individual to whom he refers had retained his residence in Canada, though he might spend eight or nine months of the year, in Florida, for his health, or for some other purpose. If his bona fide residence were in Canada he would continue to be taxed here. But this proposed amendment is to meet the hardship involved in the case of a man who bona fide changes his residence during a taxation year, the man who is an executive of a Canadian concern for the first four or five months of the year and then transfers to the American parent company.

I cite that as an example. He changes his residence from Ottawa or Montreal, as the case may be, to some place in the United States. Under the law as it stood, he would have been obliged to file an income tax return in Canada and be taxed on the total income for that calendar year, and would be entitled to claim a credit against that tax for any tax he might pay in the United States with respect to taxes paid to that government. But in some cases that was found to create injustice. One such case was cited by the hon. member for Davenport. This section is, therefore, a relieving measure and is intended to provide an equitable basis for taxation of individuals who bona fide change residence during the course of the taxing year.

On the matter of discretions, of course that is something on which a good deal has been said in this committee.
I must confess that if hon. members look far enough back in Hansard they will see that I had something to say about it myself four or five years ago. The general rule of law, as members of the bar know, is that where a discretion is given to a person under a statute and that discretion is exercised bona fide by the official or deputy minister or whoever it may be who is called upon to exercise it, the courts will not interfere with such exercise. The very words themselves, "the exercise of a discretion" imply that the individual to whom the discretion is given exercises that discretion; and the courts do not review it. The same thing applies in municipal law, for instance, where a city council is granted discretion to issue or refuse a permit for certain purposes. The courts will not issue a writ of mandamus to compel them to do so and will not review the exercise of that discretion unless it is shown that it has been influenced by improper motives. There has been a good deal of criticism of the discretionary powers given under the income war tax act to the minister.
It is riddled with them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

It was not one confined to too technical procedure. Business people appeared before it, as well as persons represented by counsel. I believe there was no fault whatsoever to find with the procedure.
But unless the minister is prepared to say that the minister took advantage of his power to reject the advice tendered to him by those boards of review, then I say the minister might as well tell us now that such boards ought to be given power, not simply to advise, but to overrule or to vary assessments.
There is the position. Unless these boards are going to make mistakes; unless they are going to go astray, if they are boards which will be composed of competent men, then I suggest that there is no reason why their functions should be confined to the tendering of advice to the minister.
The second qualification as to the scope of resolution 8 is, as I said earlier, that there is still no appeal from the exercise of discretionary powers. But those two qualifications are not the only ones which are objectionable. The third is this, that there is still no attempt being made 'this year to whittle down or to reduce the number of discretionary powers.	That is a serious
situation.
I do not need to repeat what I said earlier about the unfairness of a situation in which a taxpayer entering a contest against the Minister of National Revenue is beaten before he starts, so long as the minister can invoke one of these discretionary powers. He is just licked before he starts, if the minister is permitted to invoke one of these eighty-eight discretionary powers given him under the Income War Tax Act. I do not think any government can justify placing itself in a position of such vast superiority over those individual citizens who are called upon to pay taxes and who think they have been unjustly assessed.
That is a situation which, I submit, is so acute that it should not have to wait for another year for remedial action on the part of the government or parliament. It is just as important as those matters with respect to which the government, under resolutions 7 and 8, is proposing to take action-in resolution 7 a good step, and in resolution 8 a most inadequate one.
I urge upon the minister that it is not too late for the government to reconsider resolution 8 and, combining it with resolution 7, to give to the income tax advisory board power to review the exercise of discretionary powers by the Minister of National Revenue; to make it more in that respect than simply an advisory power; to give it real powers.
In the third place, the government should get down to business with respect to this problem of discretionary powers, because it is a problem which is so urgent that it cannot be left deferred. That is my appeal to the acting minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
On the first point raised
by the hon. member, I have already answered by saying that to create this appeal court with powers to review the discretion of the minister would be a negation of the doctrine of ministerial responsibility. It was for that same reason that the special board on war contracts depreciation and that on excess profits were made advisory boards.
In the same way this question was given most careful consideration by the government, and it was decided that it could not
Income War Tax

depart from the principle of ministerial responsibility, where discretionary power is given under the act. This board, therefore, as were other boards, must be an advisory board. As I said earlier, the exchequer court of Canada or any other court cannot and would not to-day review the exercise of discretion conferred upon a minister of the crown under a federal statute.
That is w'hy I said something must be done to confine these discretionary powers.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
On the other point, I
pointed out what the Minister of Finance said in his budget speech, that every effort would be made by the committee which, I understand, is proceeding with the revision of the Income War Tax Act, to reduce the number of discretionary powers. The committee must realize that with a complex income tax structure such as we have, efficient administration requires that a considerable measure of discretion be given to the executive branch of government.

I am not going to continue to argue the legal point about the minister's discretion, in connection with which I have no doubt he is correct, but I want to ask him one practical question. It seems to me that resolution 8 does not produce very much. As I understand it, the minister exercises discretion and then, if objection is made, the board comes in.
-Mr. ABBOTT: That is correct.
They are going to advise whether he was wrong?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right.
I do not think that is going to produce anything. After all, no minister is likely to admit that he was wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, yes, we do.

Not in this lower world. It seems to me that this is locking the door after the horse is stolen. I really do not think anything is going to happen under resolution 8. I have never been a minister, and I have no doubt that when one does become a minister he puts aside many of his lower qualities. I take it that when the minister has exercised his discretion it will take some drastic action to make him change. I am putting this forward seriously and not in an effort to make difficulty. I think we all want to bring about 
something practicable. I maintain that this board will be coming in too late, after the minister has exercised discretion. It would seem to me to be much more sensible if the board were to come in at an earlier stage. I do not take such a favourable view of this board as does the hon. member for Eglinton. The minister said in his speech, as reported on page 2923 of Hansard'.
The proposed board will decide questions of fact and law in the same manner as any other court.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is the appeal board.

I am talking about the appeal board.
It will not, however, have the power to exercise or review the discretions vested in the Minister of National Revenue by the Income War Tax Act.
There again, if the minister has exercised discretion, unless he has been palpably wrong, will the findings of the board have any effect upon discretion that he has already exercised? Is he going to go back and say that he was all wrong?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The powers of this board with respect to the discretionary powers exercised by the minister will be exactly the same as those exercised to-day by the exchequer court of Canada, or any other court for that matter. If it happened to be a federal matter it would come to the exchequer court, but in the province of Quebec, where discretion is given to local authorities by a number _ of statutes, the power would be exercised by the superior court with appeal to the court of appeal. The point which I made earlier, and which I think my hon. friend appreciated, was that the court does not review the discretion exercised by the person to whom it is entrusted. It deals with the question of whether the discretion was properly exercised. This board will have that, power and there will be further appeal to the exchequer court.
As I said a moment ago, it seems to me that this is all too late; it is locking the door after the horse is stolen; it is acting after the discretion has been exercised.

If a taxpayer asks the
minister to submit his problem to this income tax advisory board, will the decision of the board, whether it be in approval or disapproval of the minister's discretion, be a matter of record so that it may be taken as a precedent for other cases? Will it be a matter of public information, or will it be considered as merely departmental advice and not for public use?

Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I must confess that I have not given my hon. friend's question any consideration, but offhand I would think the report should be available as a precedent.
I should like to give the matter some consideration and perhaps deal a little . more fully with it when we come to the section of the bill providing for the creation of this board.

The tax appeal board is
to be a court of record and all the decisions given will be available and useful for the future, but here is a board dealing with the discretion of the minister. A taxpayer may complain and ask the minister to place his case before the advisory board. He may then not be able to find out the reaction of that advisory board unless its decisions are made a matter of public record.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
One of the questions that
would have to be considered is the matter of secrecy. At the present time, when a case is taken to the exchequer court a taxpayer may ask that the general proceedings be not made public. Of course the judgment has to be.

I had in mind the very thing the hon. member for Carleton has spoken about. I am afraid we are making too much of this matter of secrecy. It is quite all right not to publish to the world a person's private business, but where a matter is of such importance that it has to go before the minister or before a court it becomes a matter of public concern. The law is quite clear. The minister is really the judge in the first instance. He exercises discretion and that discretion becomes law. That law can be changed only by this parliament. As the hon. member for Carleton says, it is important that everyone knows what that discretion is so that he may be governed accordingly. Take the discretion in connection with double depreciation as an example. You will have to consider whether or not that should be made public so that people will know how to act. It is important to everyone to know how the government of Canada, through the minister, is exercising this discretion.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That can be done so long
as it is not revealing the private business of the taxpayer.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is the provision of section 81 of the Income War Tax Act, which is already part of the legislation and provides for secrecy with regard to income tax matters. The government seems to consider that provision as being sacrosanct, instead of realizing that here is a case where the validity of the section is being challenged.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It does not challenge it at
all.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I have never accepted
the validity of the section. As a matter of fact, several times I have moved an amendment to have it changed. It seems to me that the suggestion of the hon. member for High Park is a valid one. When a matter is contested the public show know the facts of the case.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The public is entitled to know the principle which is decided by this appeal board the same as it is entitled to know the principle which is decided by the exchequer court, buit all the facts which may concern the private business of the taxpayer have no general interest. I think it is perfectly proper that the secrecy rule Should be observed. The public is entitled to know the finding on the question of principle, the disposition of the appeal, whether the taxpayer is held liable or not and the reason why, but I do not think the public should be entitled to pry into private affairs.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Two or three years ago the Steel Company of Canada was involved in a labour dispute. I am not referring to the one now being considered by the standing committee on industrial relations. During the course of the dispute large advertisements appeared in newspapers across Canada over the name of the company, attacking the position of the union. Members of the union were anxious to know whether or not the cost of that advertising, which I submit was antiunion, was allowed as a deduction. I made an effort to secure the information, but was told that because of section 81 of this act it could not be given.. I submit there are cases like that where merely to be told the principle is not good enough; the public is entitled to know what interpretation is being made of that principle. I suggest that this whole question of secrecy should now be reviewed.

I wonder whether the minister could tell us the attitude on this point. What steps are contemplated to enable the ordinary taxpayer to know of the existence of this advisory board? Is any provision made whereby the ordinary taxpayer can obtain skilful assistance in presenting his case to the board? I think every hon. member has had a number of these matters brought to his attention, and he himself -has become more or less the advocate of his constituents before the Department of Finance. I am wondering if there is any provision, other than
Income War Tax

by a member of parliament, whereby a taxpayer can have his case presented and know just what to do?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think the measure when adopted, as I anticipate it will be, will be given wide publicity through the press. As to what steps can be taken to assist taxpayers in preparing appeals, I am afraid I am not in a position to make any statement at the moment. Possibly that can be considered a little later on.

The trouble is that the ordinary taxpayer, like the ordinary farmer, is utterly bewildered by the complexity of this whole income tax situation, and he does not know where to go to get scientific advice or assistance to present his case. The result is that he is just haunted and driven. I wonder if it is not time that we had some means of giving a little assistance to the ordinary taxpayer.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I suppose it would be indelicate for me to suggest that he should go and see a good lawyer.
The trouble with respect to going and seeing a lawyer is that there is expense involved, and the ordinary taxpayer has enough expense without going to see a lawyer.
The lawyers have to live too.

Would the minister give the committee, not necessarily to-day but perhaps to-morrow when the bill comes up, a report on the number of cases that were heard by the board of referees under section 5 of the Excess Profits Tax Act, the disposition by the minister, and the advice given to him by that board in these cases'? I think it would be interesting to the committee to know in how many cases the advice was accepted, in how many it was rejected, and in how many it was varied.
And how many cases are yet pending.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think these figures could oe obtained, and, as I said in reply to a similar question before, if they are not available when we are considering the resolutions they may be available when the Minister of National Revenue presents his estimates.
When an appeal is taken to the exchequer court, are not all the facts published in the reports of the court?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No. It is open to the taxpayer to ask that the proceedings be held in camera.

I may say it is not very often that I find myself in agreement with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre; but it seems to me that secrecy is a bit overstretched in these cases, and in the public interest I think we must, to some extent at least, if not entirely, waive the delights of secrecy in order that we may build up a body of case law, of precedents, so that taxpayers throughout the country will know where they stand, and what the decision was in any case, so that they may judge their own case accordingly.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That information can be revealed in the judgment and findings of the court without indicating names or particulars which would identify the particular parties involved. As my hon. friend probably knows, that practice is followed in the United Kingdom, I think in the United States, and probably by our own courts here.
I am not a "good lawyer"; I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: In other words, the necessary facts can be indicated in the finding of the courts to enable a proper appreciation of the judgment, without indicating the identity of the persons involved. My own feeling is that that is a proper and necessary protection. Quite a number of people might be reluctant to take an income tax appeal on a perfectly proper matter if the whole of their private affairs had to be laid before the general public; and I can see no useful purpose which would be served in doing that. I think all that is necessary is that the court should render its judgment in such form as to make clearly evident the principles on which it has proceeded in arriving at that decision; and, granted that that is done, I think that is all the public interest requires.
After listening to the explanation of the minister, which seems very satisfactory, I shall never again be tempted to agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is a bad habit.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That proves I was right.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It proves you were both wrong.

Is not the principle of secrecy one of the main planks of the income tax law? It is required that your return shall be kept secret. The minister made a facetious remark which I think had a certain amount of merit in it; he said, why not get a good lawyer to make out your income tax? Well, I, like many members of this house, have had the

Questions Dropped jrom Order Paper
pleasure of meeting civil servants employed in the income tax department, and there I had a real complaint brought to my attention, as no doubt it has been to several other members of the house, as to the amount of extra and difficult work they have to do with regard to making out the extremely complicated present income tax reforms, despite all the efforts at simplification. These people are greatly overworked, and I suggest that some consideration be given to a deduction from the income tax to enable taxpayers to employ, I will not say a "good lawyer", but counsel to make out their income tax return. It would greatly simplify the work of the Department of National Revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Speaking as a lawyer I find my hon. friend's suggestion interesting. I do not know that it would be practicable.

I think I must be drawn into this fray. Many people come to me and ask me to help them make out their income tax returns because, I believe, lawyers as a rule do not want to take the time and trouble of making these out.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: The form is so simple now that anybody can make it out.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Carried.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Do I understand that resolutions 7 and 8 are carried?

They are carried.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS COMMITTEE-REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN OTTAWA "JOURNAL".
speechtext:
Just before we adjourn, I have been instructed by the special committee on veterans affairs to raise a question of privilege. The Ottawa Journal in its leading editorial of July 24 has this to say:
Job Preference for Veterans
Against the considered advice of Mr. Charles H. Bland, chairman of the civil service commission, and Mr. Walter S. Woods, Deputy Minister of Veterans Affairs, a majority of members of the veterans affairs committee of the commons favour extension of the veterans preference for government jobs to men whose service has been confined to Canada during the war years. Since before the end of world war I this preference lias applied only to men and women with overseas service.
I suppose that is based on a report in the same paper of Monday July 22, which has a
subheading:
Would include Crown Companies, Government Agencies.
C.S. Chairman and Deputy Minister Oppose Move.
The move to extend the preference to crown companies and government agencies was not opposed by the chairman of the civil service commission and the deputy minister, and it was actually embodied in a resolution reported to this house in Votes and Proceedings of Tuesday, July 23. Our committee recommended as follows:
that the present civil service preference for disabled veterans and veterans who served overseas be extended to cover all employment both temporary and permanent, by dominion government agencies, inclusive of crown companies.
That was not opposed by the deputy minister or by the committee. The report says, however:
The committee while delaying its decision to the final report, favoured such action.
That is, widening the preference to include all home service personnel who joined the armed forces on a voluntary basis. The report states that our committee favoured that action.
The point I wish to make is that the only decision which we arrived at was reported to the house. We made no decision to extend the preference to those whose service had been confined to Canada during the war. No decision in that regard was made by the committee. That matter is still under consideration, and it is felt that this correction should be made for fear it might be thought that the committee has already come to a decision on the question. The committee felt that the newspaper reports have so far been accurate and satisfactory, and it is quite distasteful to us to draw attention to this apparent misunderstanding.
